source.title: DIVER-1: Scaling Intracranial EEG Foundation Models for Transferable Representations
source.authors: Danny Dongyeop Han; Yonghyeon Gwon; Ahhyun Lucy Lee; Taeyang Lee; Seongjin Lee; Jubin Choi; Se-Bin Lee; J. Bang; Seung-Ju Lee; David Keetae Park; Shinjae Yoo; Chun-Kee Chung; Jiook Cha

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The header identifies it as v3 dated 23 May 2026, although the supplied year is 2025.
record.tranche_reason: Applies scaling-law analyses to self-supervised intracranial EEG pretraining, a different modality and training regime, and reports scaling and compute-allocation results.
record.gate_note: The scaling sweeps, fitted loss laws, compute-allocation analysis, and downstream scaling results are the study's own results and are recorded below. Claims about language-model scaling, architecture ablations, and downstream benchmark performance not tied to scale are not treated as scaling-law results. The paper also cites prior language-model scaling results, which are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own scaling sweeps and data-constrained law fits for self-supervised iEEG masked-reconstruction pretraining (13M–1.83B parameters, 1–64 epochs, 1–100% data). This is a new modality and a repeated-data regime, so it bears on V5. Its granularity-dependent exponents and domain-dependent compute split bear on V7. Its downstream AUROC scaling bears on V6 in the iEEG setting. It does not test language-model loss, so V1–V4 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that iEEG pretraining is data-constrained: unique data and longer training matter more than parameter count. Their recipe is data first, longer training second, and model size last. They also claim that data-constrained scaling laws generalize to neural data.
record.recipe_differences: This is an iEEG masked multi-domain reconstruction study, not language-model next-token cross-entropy scaling. It applies fixed-duration sweeps and a data-constrained law with effective data and parameter counts, and studies training passes over a fixed corpus.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ by patch granularity: the fitted exponents and fit quality differ between 1s and 0.1s models. Very large 1s models can have higher loss at short durations; the authors also note possible sensitivity to model aspect ratio and sampling density.

fits_no_version.finding: Under fixed total pretraining volume, downstream AUROC varies non-monotonically with the number of pretraining subjects (2–16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subject or source diversity at fixed data volume affects downstream transfer of pretrained models in a non-monotonic way.

record.code_released: link (URL not provided in the text)
record.problems: The study concerns iEEG reconstruction rather than language-model cross-entropy. Its scaling fits are based on limited configurations: the authors report 30 configurations versus 93 in the referenced study, note that empirical iso-loss contours are less smooth due primarily to sampling density, and report lower fit reliability for the 0.1s dataset axis. Some scaling outcomes are described qualitatively from figures without numeric values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible scaling result was left out. Cited results from language-model scaling papers were excluded because they are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: All of it: no language-model held-out cross-entropy is measured.
All of it: no law is fitted on small runs and checked against runs orders of magnitude larger.
All of it for language models: the iEEG allocation analysis is recorded under V7. No allocation exponents for parameters and tokens are reported.
All of it: depth is fixed at 12 and only width varies. Shapes are not compared at fixed parameter count.
Image, video, fine-tuning and transfer scaling are untested. Only iEEG masked reconstruction, including repeated data, is tested.
Predictability of downstream performance from pretraining loss, and any LM downstream scaling.
Parameter-counting conventions, schedule choice and fitting method are not varied.

missing.what: Downstream AUROC versus pretraining corpus size with the architecture fixed: speech 0.710 (1.1%), 0.840 (17.7%), 0.847 (70.6%). Gains flatten at the largest scale.
Frozen 0.1s model sizes Tiny/Small/Large/XL give near-identical Neuroprobe AUROC, e.g. onset 0.930/0.926/0.928/0.930.
MAYO seizure AUROC across 1s model sizes is non-monotonic: frozen 0.935/0.904/0.911/0.937/0.914 for Tiny to XL.
Data-repetition half-lives R*_D = 9.54 and R*_N = 3.39 (1s); 19.7 and 0.72 (0.1s). Repeated data stays useful for many epochs.

record.verdict_notes: The study's own text is the source of all verdicts; no row here is a cited result. The allocation in R5/R6 is derived from the fitted law at two epochs, not measured optima. The authors themselves note that the aggregate multi-epoch fit gives balanced exponents, comparable to the LM replication (α 0.348, β 0.366), while the fixed two-epoch allocation is data-heavy. The record's V3 links were moved to V5/V7 because the analysis concerns iEEG, not LM token allocation. Fit R2 values are modest and sampling is sparse (about 30 configurations). The XXL anomaly may reflect µP or aspect-ratio issues rather than scaling.

versions.untested_parts: The study is on iEEG, not language models, and does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy.
The study does not report fitting a law only on small runs and then testing its loss predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.

The study analyzes iEEG data–model and parameter–training-duration allocations, not the language-model parameter/token allocation under the original abundant-data setup. It does not report explicit power exponents for both optimal parameter and token counts as functions of compute.
The scaling experiments vary width/model size with depth held fixed; they do not compare architectures at fixed parameter count.
Only iEEG masked-reconstruction pretraining is tested; image, video, repeated-data outside this iEEG setting, fine-tuning, and transfer-learning scaling are not tested.
The study reports downstream performance against dataset size, model size, training duration, and subject count, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss.
The study shows differences between its two patch granularities and undertraining effects, but does not systematically vary parameter-count conventions, training schedules, or fitting methods.

rows.note: The authors say the dataset-axis fit is less stable at this granularity and caution that the small β should be read as reduced fit reliability, not as evidence that data scaling is unhelpful.

rows.subject: DIVER-1-1s model family
rows.operation_detail: Measured loss across model sizes at short training durations.
rows.measure: Held-out pretraining loss as model size increases
rows.baseline: Smaller model variants in the same short-duration sweeps; exact values not stated.
rows.value: The XXL model has substantially higher loss when trained for only a few epochs, although the general earlier-epoch trend is decreasing loss with increasing model size.
rows.note: The authors suggest insufficient updates as an explanation and also note that the XXL aspect ratio may be outside the stable-loss region.
rows.check: Drop V7. This concerns a single model (XXL) at 2–8 epochs. The authors attribute it to insufficient updates or an unstable aspect ratio, i.e. training is the bottleneck. It is not a fitting-choice dependence.

rows.subject: DIVER-1-1s model family
rows.operation_detail: Estimated compute-optimal data–model allocation from the fitted scaling law.
rows.measure: Predicted fold-increase allocated to dataset size and parameter count
rows.value: Optimal scaling assigns > 5 × 10^7 × to dataset size and < 20× to model size.
rows.note: The paper describes this as strongly data-leaning and contrasts it with the Kaplan language-model fit. It does not state allocation exponents.
rows.check: The allocation is predicted from the fitted law at a fixed two epochs and is not a measured optimum. It bears on V7: the split depends on domain and data, being strongly data-leaning versus Kaplan's parameter-leaning split. It is iEEG, not the LM allocation V3 names, so drop V3.

rows.subject: DIVER-1-1s model family
rows.operation_detail: Estimated the compute-efficient tradeoff between model size and training duration with a fixed corpus.
rows.measure: Held-out loss across parameter count and number of training passes; compute-optimal allocation
rows.value: The efficient frontier favors small-to-mid-sized models trained for more passes over the largest models trained briefly.
rows.note: The paper says fitted-law contours reproduce the frontier; this is a parameter–duration tradeoff, not a parameter–token allocation.
rows.check: Drop V3. This is a parameter–epoch tradeoff on a fixed iEEG corpus, consistent with data-constrained (repeated-data) scaling. It is not the LM parameter/token allocation.

relationships.condition: iEEG masked-reconstruction pretraining, 1s and 0.1s families, fixed-duration sweeps and repeated-data fits
relationships.reason: Loss falls roughly linearly on log–log axes with compute, data and size (R1). The data-constrained law fits both families (R2). Predicted iso-loss contours match the empirical ones (R8, R9). The fixed-corpus frontier follows repeated-data scaling (R7).
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreased approximately as power laws in compute, data and model size, while data-constrained fits described both temporal families, matched iso-loss contours and captured the fixed-corpus frontier.

relationships.condition: 0.1s fit quality; largest 1s model at short durations
relationships.reason: The 0.1s fit has R2 of about 0.77 and an unstable data axis (R3). DIVER-1-1s XXL has substantially higher loss at 2–8 epochs, breaking the size trend (R4). Fits overall have R2 of only 0.76–0.82.
relationships.display_finding: The 0.1s fit had R² ≈ 0.77 with unstable data scaling, overall R² was 0.76–0.82, and DIVER-1-1s XXL had substantially higher loss at 2–8 epochs.
